name: Carla Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and anything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the foreperson for an interiors contractor, so we do office and shop fit-outs. A landlord hands over an empty concrete floor and we turn it into offices: metal stud walls, plasterboard, suspended ceilings, doors. Right now it's the third floor of an insurance building, twelve of us, and I'm the one with the drawings, the laser level and the phone that never stops ringing. Mornings I set out the walls on the floor with chalk lines, afternoons I'm chasing deliveries and checking boards are fixed right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the speed. You walk in on a Monday and it's a car park in the sky, and three weeks later people are arguing about who gets the window desk. What's tough is that clients change their minds every week, and I've got two lads who'd rather be on their phones. My husband Tomás is a plumber with his own van, so we compare horror stories at dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I use one to tidy up emails to project managers, because I write like I talk, and that doesn't always go down well. I tried it for working out board quantities once and it got it wrong, so I went back to my spreadsheet. I'll use it more when it's proven itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it writes my emails nicer, that's about it. At work nobody would really notice. I don't post much online, maybe I'd share a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plan stays the plan. I'm fifty-eight, house is paid off, we've got savings and a little cabin by the lake, and I was going to stop at sixty-two or sixty-three. Nothing in this changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Finish the insurance job, pick up the next one. Keep using the email thing, keep my spreadsheet for the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Relieved about what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring I went to a trade show with my boss, and there was a robot that sprays and sands the joints on plasterboard. It was slow but it worked. In this picture that thing stays a toy at a trade show, and I'd be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucía's an accountant, so I'd tell her she's safe for now. She's always told me her job's the one that'll go first. I'd tease her about it.

S0.say: AI writes her emails nicer and that's about it. Nobody at work would notice, and she might share a joke online.
S0.think: Her plan stays the plan: house paid off, savings, a lake cabin, and stopping at sixty-two or sixty-three.
S0.do: Keeps working, finishes the insurance fit-out and moves to the next job. Keeps the AI for emails and her own spreadsheet for quantities.
S0.quote: In this picture that thing stays a toy at a trade show, and I'd be glad.
S0.fieldNote: Carla is practical and money-safe, and this scenario changes nothing for her. Her relief points to a real memory: seeing a plasterboard finishing robot at a trade show. She judges AI tools on whether they've been proven, after one gave her wrong quantities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, because I've seen what's coming for interiors. At work I'd tell the younger ones to learn to work with the machines. To friends I'd say it's not the end of the world, it's just a new tool, like the laser level was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think fit-out is more exposed than people think. It's repetitive, flat floors, straight walls, same boards every time, that's the stuff robots like. I'd probably be fine, I'm the one who plans and checks, but half my crew does the kind of work that robot at the trade show did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once two or three other firms were using the robots and it was working, I'd push my boss to try one on a job, so we weren't left behind. I'd get properly comfortable with the planning software, maybe the firm pays for a course. And I'd keep putting money aside, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm all right, but I've got twelve people looking at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, he's fifty, he tapes and fills joints, he's the best I've seen. And that's exactly what the robot did. I'd want him running the machine, not watching it from the car park.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push your boss to try a robot. Isn't that the thing that would hurt Gary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I've thought about that. If we don't, another firm will and we'll lose the contracts, then everyone's out, not just Gary. Better we do it and keep him on to run it.

S1.say: Get ready, because interiors work is coming next. She'd tell younger workers to learn the machines and friends that it's just a new tool, like the laser level.
S1.think: Fit-out is more exposed than people think because it's flat, straight and repetitive. She'd be fine as the planner and checker, but half her crew does work the trade-show robot already did.
S1.do: Pushes her boss to trial a robot once two or three other firms have it working, and takes a firm-paid course in planning software. Keeps saving as now.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with twelve people looking to her.
S1.quote: I'd want him running the machine, not watching it from the car park.
S1.fieldNote: Carla is unusually clear about her own trade's exposure, based on what she saw at a trade show. She accepts a contradiction openly: she'd bring in the robot that threatens her best taper, reasoning it protects the firm. Her steady temperament shows in waiting for other firms to prove it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is a big step up. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy and nobody's ready. At work I'd say keep your heads down, do good work, and save your money. I wouldn't post much, I don't like shouting into the void.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be finished at sixty, maybe before. My job is planning and checking, and AI that can do anything can read a drawing and set out walls. We'd be okay with what we've got, but I'd lose my best earning years and I'd worry about what happens to the house prices and the cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Tomás and go through every account. We'd cut back, no new car, put off redoing the cabin roof. I'd talk to my boss about a way out on decent terms, and I'd move some savings into cash so it's there if the markets go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, we'd survive, but my stomach would be in knots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you'd better hope robots can't fit a toilet, because you might be the one paying the bills for a while. He'd laugh. Then we'd both go quiet, because neither of us actually knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your son in the army?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Diego, yes. I'd worry about him in a different way, because who knows what a world like that does to armies. I'd want him home. But he's thirty, he'd do what he thinks is right.

S2.say: This will be messy and nobody's ready. She'd tell the crew to keep their heads down, do good work and save their money.
S2.think: She expects to be finished at sixty or sooner, because AI that can do anything can read a drawing and set out walls. They'd be okay, but she'd lose her best earning years and worry about the value of the house and cabin.
S2.do: Goes through every account with her husband in the first month and cuts back, skipping a new car and the cabin roof. Negotiates a decent exit with her boss and moves some savings into cash.
S2.feel: Anxious, stomach in knots, but sure they'd survive.
S2.quote: I'd say, you'd better hope robots can't fit a toilet, because you might be the one paying the bills for a while.
S2.fieldNote: Even with strong savings, the fast case makes Carla cautious and defensive with money. Her humour with her husband turns quickly to silence, which says more than her words. Worry about her son in the army is a separate, harder-to-name fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time, so let's be sensible. At work I'd push for a proper plan for the crew. To friends, I'd say don't panic, but don't ignore it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three, about when I'd planned to stop anyway. So for me it's almost like a natural end. It's the crew, and Lucía, that I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the planning software properly, maybe the robot side too, so I could help the firm through the first couple of years. I'd talk to our adviser about putting some savings into the companies making the machines, a small bet. And I'd help Lucía think about where an accountant goes when the computer does the accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It feels like there's time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy shares in the robot companies. How does that sit with worrying about your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's just sensible. If the machines are coming either way, I might as well have a little piece of it. It doesn't stop me fighting for Gary to keep his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucía say, if you asked her what she'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she's already looking at moving into something with people, like advising small businesses face to face. She's smarter than me about this. I'd tell her she has my blessing and a bit of money if she needs it.

S3.say: Five years gives time, so let's be sensible. She'd push for a proper plan for the crew and tell friends not to panic but not to ignore it.
S3.think: She'd be sixty-three, about when she'd planned to stop, so it's a natural end for her. Her worry is the crew and her daughter.
S3.do: Learns the planning software and the robot side properly to help the firm through the transition. Puts a small part of savings into companies making the machines and helps her daughter plan a move toward face-to-face advice work.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, with time to think.
S3.quote: If the machines are coming either way, I might as well have a little piece of it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Carla's steady pragmatism take over: learn, invest a little, help her daughter. She doesn't see buying robot shares as disloyal to her crew. She trusts her daughter's judgement more than her own on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so if people get caught out it's their own fault or the government's. At work I'd say learn the machines now. I'd probably say it once and then get on with my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, at the cabin as much as possible. My kids are grown and would have plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned and stop at sixty-two or sixty-three. I'd keep the small investment in the robot companies and maybe add to it. And I'd make sure Gary and the younger ones knew what was coming early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's far enough away that I can think about it like the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if people get caught out it's their fault or the government's. Which one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. Ten years is a long time to ignore something. But the government should be making sure there's training and help, people can't do it all on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most, if you imagine a fit-out done by robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setting out, I think. Standing on an empty floor with a chalk line and seeing the whole office in my head before anything's built. If a robot does that, fine, but it won't enjoy it like I do.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so getting caught out would be people's own fault or the government's. She'd tell the crew to learn the machines now, once, and get on with her day.
S4.think: At sixty-eight she'd be retired and at the lake cabin as much as possible, and her grown children would have plenty of time.
S4.do: Retires as planned at sixty-two or sixty-three and keeps, perhaps adds to, her small investment in robot companies. Warns her crew early about what's coming.
S4.feel: Calm, thinking about it like the weather.
S4.quote: Standing on an empty floor with a chalk line and seeing the whole office in my head before anything's built.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Carla is calm and her pragmatism shows in splitting blame between people and government. What she'd miss is the craft of setting out, not the money. Her investment idea from the five-year case carries through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Losing those last good years of earning, and not knowing what my house and savings are worth. What would help is clear information early, honest numbers from the government about what's coming, and some help for people over fifty who get pushed out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the clients will feel. Nobody wants a cheaper office if the people in it are all worried about their own jobs. I've built a lot of offices, and I've never once seen a happy one that was half empty.

headlineQuote: I've built a lot of offices, and I've never once seen a happy one that was half empty.
portrait: Carla Lopez is a 58-year-old foreperson on office and shop fit-outs, married to a self-employed plumber, with a paid-off house, savings and a lake cabin. She uses AI now and then for emails but trusts her own spreadsheet for numbers. Having seen a plasterboard finishing robot at a trade show, she knows her trade is more exposed than people think and worries most for her best taper, Gary. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious and defensive with money, cutting spending and negotiating an exit. With more time she'd learn the tools, make a small investment in robot companies, and help her daughter move toward face-to-face work.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, losing her last good earning years and not knowing what her house and savings would be worth.
whatWouldHelp: Clear, honest numbers from the government early on, and help for people over fifty who get pushed out.
